notes.text: Then Peter standing up — All the gestures, all the words of Peter, show the utmost sobriety; lifted up his voice - With cheerfulness and boldness; and said to them - This discourse has three parts; each of which, ver. 14, 22, 29, begins with the same appellation, men: only to the last part he prefixes with more familiarity the additional word brethren. Men of Judea - That is, ye that are born in Judea. St. Peter spoke in Hebrew, which they all understood.
Lord — Jesus, after his exaltation, is constantly meant by this word in the New Testament, unless sometimes where it occurs, in a text quoted from the Old Testament.
They said to the apostles, Brethren — They did not style them so before.

Repent — And hereby return to God: be baptized - Believing in the name of Jesus - And ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost - See the three-one God clearly proved. See chap. xxvi, 20. The gift of the Holy Ghost does not mean in this place the power of speaking with tongues. For the promise of this was not given to all that were afar off, in distant ages and nations. But rather the constant fruits of faith, even righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. Whomsoever the Lord our God shall call - (Whether they are Jews or Gentiles) by his word and by his Spirit: and who are not disobedient to the heavenly calling. But it is observable St. Peter did not yet understand the very words he spoke.

And with many other words did he testify and exhort — In such an accepted time we should add line upon line, and not leave off, till the thing is done. Save yourselves from this perverse generation - Many of whom were probably mocking still.
And there were added — To the hundred and twenty.

glossa.text: *Jewish men.* That is, there are two causes of prudence, namely that they were Jews, and that they dwelt in Jerusalem, which sobriety becomes.

*Him Lord.* Setting down the name of majesty and of power, he shows him to be one to whom every creature ought to be subjected. Christ is the name of royal or of pontifical dignity. In the law kings and pontiffs were anointed, in a figure of him. *And Christ.* He is truly Christ, anointed with all the fulness of the Holy Spirit, who of the same Spirit gave powerfully to whom he would. *Jesus whom,* etc. Jesus is Lord and Christ, one person existing in two natures, because born eternally of the Father in the Divinity, made temporally in the humanity, when by the working of the Holy Spirit he was incarnate in the womb of the virgin.

*Pricked.* The prophecy of Joel is fulfilled, because after the fire of the Holy Spirit follows the vapour of compunction. Smoke is wont to draw out tears, they begin to weep who had mocked, they beat the breast, they give prayer to God as a sacrifice, that they may be able to taste that blood, to be saved by him, which they had before called down upon themselves and upon their sons.
*In the name.* In the honour, or in this form, because in one the faith of the three is contained.

*And to all.* This is referred to that testimony of prophecy which he set last, namely *Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved:* which pertains especially to the calling of the Gentiles; who, made far off from the children of Israel, were to be saved through the invocation of the name of the Lord.

*He testified,* etc., that is, testimony and exhortation. *Save yourselves.* This is the quality of the testimony and of the exhortation, but Luke concluded very many words of Peter in a brief sentence. *From the generation.* There are two generations, one of the good, the other of the wicked.

notes.text: The sorrows — Dangerous and deadly calamities. Pains - Such agonies and horrors, as dying persons use to feel.

glossa.text:
*I have loved.* ((ID.)) This the sheep says which had strayed, the son returned, the pilgrim of this world.

((CASS.)) *I have loved.* Not for the temporal goods given to me, as the unbelievers do, but *because,* etc. God is loved even by unbelievers because he gives good things; whence: *I will praise thee when thou shalt do well to him ((Psal. XLVIII))*. He is loved perfectly, him *eum*; read *cum*, "when" the mind is not moved by adverse things, but is kindled by hope: which manner he afterwards expounds, *I have loved.* Not because he made me a king, or gave me prosperity, but because he hears my prayer in straits.

*And in my days.* ((AUG.)) Namely of my misery, which days I made for myself by sinning, which are full of labour and sorrow, that is, of the old rottenness.

*I will call upon.* Which is not without faith; whence the Apostle: *How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? ((Rom. X.))* When therefore he says, *they shall call upon,* note that the lover is not idle. In which, *They have compassed me,* etc. Or, in the days of salvation, that is, in the time of fulness; whence: *Behold, now is the acceptable time,* etc. ((II Cor. VI)).

*Sorrows.* ((CASS.)) Sins, whence come the sorrow and the death of the soul; or eternal sorrows, and this shall be in hell. *The perils of hell.* ((AUG.)) For, steeped in carnal pleasure, I did not perceive the evils that compassed me about.
*Trouble and sorrow.* ((ID.)) As it were: those things first compassed me about, but afterwards I found trouble and sorrow, that is, outward affliction, to be profitable.

*What shall I render to the Lord.* ((ID.))? This man, affrighted, looks back upon his own infirmity, and sees that he must not presume of himself. For of himself man is a liar, as Peter also, when he presumed, was found a liar: but it is the power of God, if he does not believe. Seeing this wrought in himself by the grace of God, he subjoins, *which he hath rendered to me.* He says not, for all the things which he hath bestowed. What goods of man, therefore, went before, that of all the gifts of God it might be called not a bestowing, but a rendering again? What had gone before but sins? God therefore renders to men good things for evil, having suffered for them, whereas men render evil things for good.

*The chalice of salvation.* ((ID.)) The passion, from a likeness, etc., *as far as* which is said afterwards.

((CASS.)) *The chalice,* because it is drunk under measure. Whence, *God is faithful, who suffereth you not to be tempted above that which ye are able ((I Cor. X))*. *Of salvation,* because it is propitious unto eternal salvation.

*Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.* ((AUG.)) He who suffered first grants that his own sufferings be imitated; and therefore: *Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.* He bought it with the blood which he shed for them, that they might not doubt to die for him. Bought therefore at this price, he confesses his own condition: *O Lord, for I,* etc.

*O Lord, for,* etc. ((CASS.)) Secondly they call themselves servants, and sons of the Church, because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, lest any of the heretics should think his martyrdom to be pleasing to God. *O Lord.* He wonders that he has received such things as the Lord received for the redemption of the world. And to increase the wonder he repeats: *I am thy servant. The son of the handmaid.* ((AUG.)) Of the heavenly Jerusalem, free from sins, the handmaid of justice. But they who are outside the Church are not sons of the handmaid, even though they call themselves servants (because they have the name of Christ) and martyrs, as the heretics do. *The son of the handmaid,* Not a schismatic. Or, as a handmaid brings forth not for herself, but for the Lord; so I too in my death shall bring forth some for thee, as also in my life.

*Thou hast broken my bonds.* ((CASS.)) By the power of martyrdom the bonds of sins are broken, because all things are washed away by the blood. This verse is believed by some to be of such power that a man's sins are forgiven, if at the end of his life it be said with a threefold confession.

((ID.)) Who *precious. O Lord, to thee will I sacrifice;* speaking to God, he affirms what he had said above.

*I will sacrifice.* ((AUG., CASS.)) And because thou hast broken them, to thee will I sacrifice, as one that is thankful, *The sacrifice of praise.* So that:

*I will pay *reddum* my vows.* Not everywhere, but *in the courts,* that is, in the Catholic Church, not in that of the heretics. *Of the house of the Lord.* He shows which it is.

*In the sight of all the people.* ((CASS.)) He ought to be praised publicly who was willing to suffer for all, that the more may be edified. *I will pay my vows.* Myself, who am the image of God, which must be rendered to God, etc., *as far as* and here he names Jerusalem more openly. ((AUG.)) But lest *ue* any think that by Jerusalem the Jews alone are signified, who glory in this name, let him hear the following psalm *Psalmus*; read *Psalmum*, "the following psalm": *Praise the Lord, all ye nations.* These are the courts of the Lord, for that is the people.

notes.text: Who judgeth according to every man's work — According to the tenor of his life and conversation. Pass the time of your sojourning - Your short abode on earth. In humble, loving fear - The proper companion and guard of hope.
Your vain conversation — Your foolish, sinful way of life.
Without blemish — In himself. Without spot - From the world.

Who through him believe — For all our faith and hope proceed from the power of his resurrection. In God that raised Jesus, and gave him glory - At his ascension. Without Christ we should only dread God; whereas through him we believe, hope, and love.

Having purified your souls by obeying the truth through the Spirit, who bestows upon you freely, both obedience and purity of heart, and unfeigned love of the brethren, go on to still higher degrees of love. Love one another fervently — With the most strong and tender affection; and yet with a pure heart - Pure from any spot of unholy desire or inordinate passion.
Which liveth — Is full of divine virtue. And abideth the same forever.

glossa.text:
*In fear,* etc. ((HIER.)) I, defiled with all the filth of sins, day and night await with trembling to pay the last farthing. And the time when it shall be said to me, Jerome, come forth.

*Of your sojourning.* That you may be able to be holy, have your conversation in fear, in the time of your sojourning, so long as you are in the exile of this world. *For blessed is he that is always fearful,* this I say if you call upon God, as if he should say: You do not truly call upon God, unless you be solicitous and fearful.

*But with the precious blood.* The order of the letter is: but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb uncontaminated and unspotted. Here he touches upon the Levitical and priestly celebrations. And he signifies the clean soul, through justice, which is offered to God.

notes.text: Mark xvi, 12.
Today is the third day — The day he should have risen again, if at all.
O foolish — Not understanding the designs and works of God: And slow of heart - Unready to believe what the prophets have so largely spoken.

Ought not Christ — If he would redeem man, and fulfil the prophecies concerning him, to have suffered these things? - These very sufferings which occasion your doubts, are the proofs of his being the Messiah. And to enter into his glory - Which could be done no other way.
He made as though he would go farther — Walking forward, as if he was going on; and he would have done it, had they not pressed him to stay.
They constrained him — By their importunate entreaties.
He took the bread, and blessed, and brake — Just in the same manner as when he instituted his last supper.
Their eyes were opened — That is, the supernatural cloud was removed: And he vanished - Went away insensibly.
Did not our heart burn within us — Did not we feel an unusual warmth of love! Was not our heart burning, &c.
The same hour — Late as it was.

The Lord hath appeared to Simon — Before he was seen of the twelve apostles, 1 Cor. xv, 5. He had, in his wonderful condescension and grace, taken an opportunity on the former part of that day (though where, or in what manner, is not recorded) to show himself to Peter, that he might early relieve his distresses and fears, on account of having so shamefully denied his Master.
In the breaking of bread — The Lord's Supper.

glossa.text: *Named Emmaus.* Emmaus is itself the metropolis, a notable city of Palestine, which, after the storming of Judea, was restored under the prince Marcus Aurelius Antonius, and changed its name along with its condition.

*While they talked together.* The Lord draws near and accompanies them as they speak of him, that he may both kindle in their minds the faith of the resurrection, and fulfil what he had promised he would do: *Where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them ((Matth. XXVIII))*. *Drawing near,* etc. *Their eyes,* etc. He appeared indeed in his own form, but did not show the form which they might recognize. As they both loved him within and yet doubted, so he himself is present outside and at hand, and does not show who he is. To those who speak of him, then, he grants his presence; but from those who doubt of him he takes away the appearance by which he might be known.

*Art thou a stranger,* etc. *To whom,* etc. They think him a stranger whom they do not recognize. And truly he was a stranger to them, from whose frailty he now stood far off through the glory of the resurrection, and from whose faith, ignorant of the resurrection, he remained an alien. *A man, a prophet,* etc. *And how they delivered him up,* etc. They confess him a prophet and a great one; of the Son of God they are silent, either because they do not yet believe perfectly, or, if they believe, they fear to be delivered into the hands of the Jews, not knowing with whom they speak.

*But we hoped,* etc. In a manner they refute themselves, in that they had hoped for redemption in him whom they had seen dead, nor did they believe that he would rise again; and they grieve most of all that he was slain without guilt, whom they had known to be innocent; and from this they were walking sorrowful .

*They affrighted us,* etc. They are rightly said *teruisse* those to whom they added more sadness about the body not found than they bring gladness, by the resurrection announced, wherewith they might be refreshed.

*Some of us went,* etc. Since above he said that Peter ran to the monument, and now Cleophas says: *Some of us went to the monument,* etc., it is to be understood that two went together. But he mentioned Peter alone first, because Mary announced it to him first.

*O foolish and slow of heart.* Here a twofold necessity of being humbled presses upon us, who are neither taught in the Scriptures as much as we ought, nor as intent as is fitting on fulfilling the things we know. For if Moses and the prophets spoke of Christ, and had foretold that he would enter through passion into glory, how does he glory that he is a Christian who neither searches out in the Scriptures how they pertain to Christ, nor desires to reach through sufferings the glory which he wishes to have with Christ?

*And he himself,* etc. *Stay with us,* etc. He showed himself such in body as he was among them in mind. They were to be tested, whether they would love at least as a stranger him whom they did not yet love as God. But because they cannot be strangers to the brightness, they with whom the Truth was walking call him to lodging, nay compel him. From which example it is gathered that strangers are not only to be invited to lodging, but even to be drawn in.

*He broke it,* etc. Him whom they did not know in the exposition of Scripture they knew in the breaking of bread; because not the hearers of the law but the doers shall be justified, and the truth is better understood by working than by hearing.
*Their eyes were opened,* etc. The appearance of weakness is withdrawn from the eyes of the flesh, that the glory of the resurrection may begin to appear to their minds.

*And they said,* etc. Mystically: for this reason another likeness was shown them in Christ, that they might not know him save in the breaking of bread; so that all may understand that they do not recognize Christ unless they become partakers of his body, that is, of the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of the bread, saying: *We being many are one bread, one body ((I Cor. X))*. When therefore he reaches out the blessed bread, their eyes are opened that they may know him, and the impediment is removed which was upon their eyes from Satan, that Jesus might not be recognized. And this impediment the Lord allows to remain until the sacrament of the bread be come to. But when the unity of the body has been shared, the enemy's impediment is taken away, that Christ may be recognized.

*Burning. ((GREG.))* When the word had been heard, the heart, before cold with the numbness of unbelief and of fear, was kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it now burns with a heavenly desire and stretches itself out to believe the truth. By as many precepts as a man is instructed, by so many torches, as it were, is he set aflame.

*The Lord is risen.* Already there was a report that Jesus had risen, made by those women and by Simon Peter, to whom he had appeared; these two found them speaking of these things. But they themselves also had heard earlier that he had risen; yet they feared to say it on the way, when they said only that angels had been seen by the women. For, not knowing him with whom they were speaking, they could fear that they might fall into the hands of the Jews, if they should say anything anywhere about Christ's resurrection.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit. I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day […]
echoes.note: Formal, formula-marked citation ('this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel,' v.16) reproducing Joel 2:28-32 (LXX 3:1-5) at high verbal volume: pouring out the Spirit on all flesh, sons/daughters prophesying, young men visions, old men dreams, servants and handmaids, wonders in heaven and signs on earth, blood/fire/smoke, sun to darkness and moon to blood before the great day of the Lord, and whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved. Luke's 'in the last days' adapts Joel's 'afterward.' The anchor quotation of the chapter; maximal on all three auditable tests.

echoes.text: Mount Sinai, all it, smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
echoes.note: The 'smoke' (kapnos) among the apocalyptic signs (v.19) may resonate with the smoke of Sinai where 'the mountain was wholly in smoke' at the theophany, reinforcing the Sinai-Pentecost frame. Low volume and the wording is governed by Joel; contested.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: 'Before the great and notable day of the Lord' overlaps the Malachi expectation of the great and dreadful day of the LORD; the phrase is shared eschatological idiom that Joel and Malachi both carry. Faint and mediated through Joel; contested as an independent source.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.id: The City of David and Old City, on the spurs above the Kidron Valley, c. 50 km from the Mediterranean. Pre-Israelite Jebus; named here as the seat of Adoni-Zedek, leader of the southern coalition.

places.name: Judea
places.id: The Roman administrative province (later procuratorial province) covering the southern hill country of Israel — Jerusalem, the Judean wilderness, and territory south to the Negev. The Greco-Roman successor to the Hasmonean and Herodian Iudaea. Pin sits in the central hill country.

echoes.text: This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is Yahweh’s Passover.
echoes.note: 'Gird up the loins of your mind' literalizes the Passover posture—'your loins girded, your sandals on, in haste'—readiness for imminent deliverance, fitting the redemption-by-the-lamb imagery of 1:18-19. High volume on the distinctive idiom plus contextual Passover coherence.

echoes.text: For I am Yahweh your God. Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy; for I am holy: neither shall you defile yourselves with any kind of creeping thing that moves on the earth. For I am Yahweh who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
echoes.note: Formula-marked citation ('because it is written, You shall be holy, for I am holy'). Leviticus 11:44-45 supplies the holiness ground anchored in the exodus ('I am the LORD who brought you up out of Egypt to be your God'), matching Peter's redemption framing. Highest volume—explicit quotation.

echoes.text: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.
echoes.note: 'You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy' is the most verbally exact source of 1:16 and heads the Holiness Code chapter Peter draws on repeatedly (love of neighbor, impartiality). Co-primary with Leviticus 11:44-45.

echoes.text: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.
echoes.note: 'The God of gods... who is not partial and takes no bribe' is the locus classicus for 'judges impartially, without respect of persons' (1:17). Distinctive 'shows no partiality' formula; high thematic coherence.

echoes.text: Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You shall take it from the sheep, or from the goats:
echoes.note: 'Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old' is the Passover-lamb specification behind 'a lamb without blemish or spot' (1:19), reinforcing the redemption/exodus matrix of the pericope. High volume on the without-blemish lamb.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: 'Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter... he opened not his mouth' supplies the suffering-Servant lamb whose blood ransoms; Peter fuses Passover lamb with Isaian Servant (cf. the dense Isaiah 53 citation in 2:22-25). High thematic coherence and recurrence in the letter.

echoes.text: Brace yourself like a man, for I will question you, then you answer me!
echoes.note: 'Gird up your loins like a man' (also 40:7) is the summons to brace for an encounter with God; supplies the metaphorical (mental readiness) sense Peter intends. Moderate verbal volume; the idiom recurs as a call to resolve.

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: 'You repay each according to his work' supplies the second half of 1:17 (judges 'according to each one's work'); a fixed retributive formula. Moderate volume, recurs widely.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, “You were sold for nothing; and you shall be redeemed without money.”
echoes.note: 'You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money' stands behind 'redeemed, not with silver or gold' (1:18)—redemption explicitly not monetary. Distinctive silver/gold-vs-true-redemption contrast.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: 'I will redeem you with an outstretched arm' is the exodus redemption verb Peter applies to ransom 'from the futile ways inherited from your fathers'—a new exodus from ancestral bondage. Thematic coherence high.

echoes.text: Yahweh, my strength, and my stronghold, and my refuge in the day of affliction, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, vanity and things in which there is no profit.
echoes.note: 'Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies, worthless things (vanity) in which there is no profit' closely matches 'the futile ways inherited from your fathers' (1:18)—ancestral idolatry as vanity. Notable verbal contact (inherited+vain+fathers).

echoes.text: that you may be accepted, you shall offer a male without defect, of the bulls, of the sheep, or of the goats. But whatever has a defect, that you shall not offer; for it shall not be acceptable for you.
echoes.note: The sacrificial requirement that an offering be 'without blemish... no defect' generalizes the spotless-lamb language of 1:19 across the cult. Supports volume of the blemish-free motif.

echoes.text: “You therefore put your belt on your waist, arise, and speak to them all that I command you. Don’t be dismayed at them, lest I dismay you before them.
echoes.note: 'Gird up your loins; stand and speak' commissions the prophet to fearless action; reinforces the gird-loins call but is a secondary witness to the idiom. Low distinctiveness.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD... give to each according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds' parallels the judge-by-works formula; secondary witness, low distinctiveness.

echoes.text: Think not to corrupt with gifts; for he will not receive them: And set not your mind on an unrighteous sacrifice; For the Lord is judge, And with him is no respect of persons. He will not accept any person against a poor man; And he will listen to the prayer of him that is wronged.
echoes.note: 'The Lord is judge, and with him there is no partiality' shows the impartial-judge formula in Second Temple piety, supporting the recurrence of 1:17's idea; minimal verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: 'My servant shall be exalted and lifted up' grounds 'raised him from the dead and gave him glory' (1:21)—the Servant's vindication. Faint, figural, but coherent with Peter's suffering-then-glory pattern.

echoes.text: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: Verbatim, formula-introduced citation ('For, All flesh is like grass... the grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of the Lord endures forever'). Peter quotes the LXX of Isaiah 40:6-8 to ground the imperishable seed/word; highest volume. Isaiah's word-of-comfort frames the whole exile-and-restoration ecclesiology of the letter.

echoes.text: As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes. For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.
echoes.note: 'As for man, his days are like grass; he flourishes like a flower of the field; the wind passes over it and it is gone' is a parallel grass/flower-frailty topos reinforcing the Isaiah 40 quotation. Moderate volume; same withering-flower imagery.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Love one another earnestly from the heart' (1:22) draws on the Holiness Code command 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself'—the same Leviticus 19 chapter Peter quotes for holiness in 1:16. Recurrence within the source chapter supports the link though Peter rephrases.

echoes.text: I heard the man clothed in linen, who was above the waters of the river, when he held up his right hand and his left hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives forever that it shall be for a time, times, and a half; and when they have made an end of breaking in pieces the power of the holy people, all these things shall be finished.
echoes.note: 'Living and abiding word of God' resonates with oaths by 'him who lives forever'; faint, the enduring/living quality is better anchored in the Isaiah 40 citation that follows.

echoes.text: “I, even I, am he who comforts you: who are you, that you are afraid of man who shall die, and of the son of man who shall be made as grass;
echoes.note: 'Why are you afraid of mortal man... who fades like grass?' is a nearby Isaian grass-frailty saying within the same comfort-of-Zion section, supporting the Isaiah 40 recurrence. Low distinctiveness on its own.

echoes.text: You sweep them away as they sleep. In the morning they sprout like new grass. In the morning it sprouts and springs up. By evening, it is withered and dry.
echoes.note: Humanity 'like grass that is renewed in the morning... in the evening it fades and withers' is another grass-mortality witness underlining the perishable-vs-enduring contrast of 1:23-25. Faint, thematic.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: Jesus' rebuke that the Christ 'had to suffer these things and enter into his glory' presupposes the Suffering Servant who is 'despised and rejected' yet afterward exalted (Isa 52:13; 53:11-12). Luke roots the necessity (dei) of messianic suffering in the Servant Songs, which he cites explicitly elsewhere (Lk 22:37). Coherence with the chapter's exegetical climax is strong.

echoes.text: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning? My God, I cry in the daytime, but you don’t answer; in the night season, and am not silent. But you are holy, you who inhabit the praises of Israel. Our fathers trusted in you. They trusted, and you delivered them. They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed. But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of […]
echoes.note: The motif of the righteous one who suffers grievously and is then vindicated, which Jesus expounds 'beginning from Moses and all the prophets,' draws on the Passion psalm Luke uses in the crucifixion scene. The suffering-and-glory pattern of Psalm 22 (lament turning to praise/vindication) is a primary text in the Scriptural 'things concerning himself.' Coherence high.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'Enter into his glory' echoes the enthronement of the one like a son of man who is given glory and dominion before the Ancient of Days. Luke pairs suffering with glorification, and Daniel 7 supplies the vindicated-and-glorified figure central to his messianic reading. Recurrence across the chapter supports it.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: The travelers describe Jesus as 'a prophet mighty in deed and word,' and the exposition 'beginning from Moses' invokes the prophet-like-Moses whom God would raise up and to whom Israel must listen. Luke elsewhere applies this text to Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37), making it a likely component of the Mosaic witness here. Coherence and recurrence support medium confidence.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: The risen Jesus joins the travelers unrecognized and is pressed to stay and share a meal, recalling the LORD/angels appearing to Abraham as a wayfarer who is welcomed with hospitality and food. The pattern of unrecognized divine visitor received with hospitality is a Scriptural type Luke evokes, though there is no verbal quotation. Contested, low volume.

echoes.text: He went to seek a man, and found Raphael who was an angel; and he didn’t know it. He said to him, “Can I go with you to Rages of Media? Do you know those places well?” The angel said to him, “I will go with you. I know the way well. I have lodged with our brother Gabael.” Tobias said to him, “Wait for me, and I will tell my father.” He said to him, “Go, and don’t wait. And he went in and said to his father, “Behold, I have found someone who will go with […]
echoes.note: The angel Raphael travels incognito with Tobias as an unrecognized companion whose true identity is disclosed only at the end (Tob 12). The Emmaus narrative's structure of a hidden divine guide on a journey parallels Tobit's traveling-angel motif, a recognizable Second-Temple type. Faint and structural rather than verbal, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth.
echoes.note: The report that the chief priests 'delivered him up to be condemned to death' resonates with the Servant who was 'led like a lamb to the slaughter' and handed over. As part of the Servant subtext Jesus is about to expound, it colors the travelers' summary, though without quotation. Low and somewhat contested.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, to him whom man despises, to him whom the nation abhors, to a servant of rulers: “Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall worship; because of Yahweh who is faithful, even the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you.”
echoes.note: The hope that Jesus 'would redeem Israel' sits within the Servant's mission to restore and redeem Israel before he is given as a light to the nations. Luke's redemption-of-Israel language (cf. Lk 1:68; 2:38) draws on Deutero-Isaiah's restoration vocabulary. Faint here, hence low.

echoes.text: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
echoes.note: 'Their eyes were opened, and they recognized him' deliberately inverts 'the eyes of both were opened' in Eden, where opened eyes brought shame and exile; here opened eyes at the breaking of bread bring recognition of the risen Lord. The verbal correspondence (eyes opened) plus reversal is a coherent Lukan new-creation motif. Volume is moderate; the allusion is widely recognized.

echoes.text: He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.
echoes.note: The shared meal at which the divine guest is recognized recalls the LORD/angels eating with Abraham at Mamre, where hospitality discloses the visitor's identity. The Emmaus meal as the locus of revelation parallels the Mamre table-fellowship type. Structural and faint, so low and contested.

echoes.text: They shall eat the flesh in that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs.
echoes.note: The breaking of bread that opens their eyes carries Passover/Eucharistic overtones, the meal at which deliverance is remembered and made present. Given Luke's Passover framing of the Last Supper, the Emmaus bread figurally recalls the Passover bread of redemption. Typological rather than verbal, hence low and contested.

echoes.text: Elisha prayed, and said, “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” Yahweh opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.
echoes.note: Elisha's prayer that the servant's eyes be opened to see the unseen heavenly reality offers a parallel for the divinely granted opening of eyes to perceive the risen Christ. The motif of God opening human eyes to spiritual sight is a recurring OT pattern Luke taps. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.
echoes.note: Jesus 'vanished out of their sight' faintly echoes the sudden removal of righteous figures who are 'taken' by God (Enoch 'was not, for God took him'). As a marker of a translated/heavenly figure no longer subject to ordinary presence, it anticipates the ascension. Very faint, contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: We walked away from the city, slow with grief.
He came alongside and would not leave us.
At the table he took the bread and broke it.
Our eyes were opened, and we knew him.
What can we give for all his goodness to us?
We will lift the cup of salvation.
Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: You who set out this morning heavy-hearted, with hope gone cold behind you — come and sit, for the road is not the end of the story.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
Watch his hands take the loaf, bless it, break it; the same hands that were pierced now passing you the bread.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
And there, in the breaking, the stranger is no stranger, and the grief becomes a fire that sends us running back.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
What shall we render for such goodness? We lift the cup of salvation and call upon his name.
Christ is risen, alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: We walked away heavy with grief; he drew near on the road.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
He broke the bread, and we knew him.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
What shall we give for all his goodness?
Christ is risen, alleluia!
We lift the cup of salvation. Come, let us worship.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
